Natural language processing (NLP) for question understanding: AI can help understand and interpret the intent behind user questions, even when they are not well-formulated. Personalized learning and skill development: AI can track a user's activity, preferences, and areas of expertise to provide personalized recommendations for learning resources, relevant questions, and potential collaborations. This can foster skill development and encourage community engagement.  It's worth noting that while AI can bring valuable improvements, it should be used in conjunction with human moderation and expertise to ensure the accuracy, fairness, and quality of the content on Stack Overflow. SOAI: I think there are a lot of opportunities for AI to improve Stack Overflow, mostly to help improve questions before they are posted. AI could interactively make suggestions while users are creating their questions: correcting grammar, removing salutations, suggesting what additional information might be helpful for getting a good answer (e.g. add a code sample; include the stack trace from the error you're seeing; tell people which framework you're using; clarify what you mean by "doesn't work" or "crashes"; you appear to be asking in Spanish, or looking for a code review: these other sites might be more appropriate...). It could be used to generate queries against existing questions that are more likely to yield duplicate matches than the current "related questions" feature currently provides. Depending on the nature of the question, it's possible AI could try to provide an answer to the question directly, and posting the question becomes the fall-back option if the answer seems unsatisfactory (though obviously this could be dangerous if not done well).

SOAI: I consider the use of token sequence prediction tools like ChatGPT and all of its derivative for serious knowledge engineering work to be professional malpractice. Genuinely novel questions - e.g. the kind StackOverflow derives the most benefit from - will necessarily get the poorest suggestions for titles, because those examples will be absent or underrepresented in the corpus used to train the model. Given the compute costs associated with running such models, I genuinely wonder whether your users (perhaps only those with sufficient reputation) would get more utility out of being able to run (non-Turing complete) full-text and structured queries of their own against StackOverflow's index and present those results to other users of the site.
